title: Given the root of a binary tree, imagine standing on the right side of it; return the values of the nodes visible from the right, ordered top to bottom. This is the last node of each level in a level order traversal.
shortTitle: Right View of a Binary Tree (Last Node of Each Level)
keyPoints: The right view is the last node of each level in a BFS, not just the right spine of the tree
Use the level-size snapshot technique and capture the node when index equals levelSize - 1
A left-child node can appear in the right view if the right subtree does not extend to that depth
Enqueue left before right to ensure left-to-right processing within each level
The DFS alternative visits right before left and records the first node at each new depth
Time is O(n), space is O(w) for BFS or O(h) for DFS

s1_definition.oneliner: BFS per level; capture the last node of each level into the result.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Right view** – the set of nodes visible from the right side of the tree: one per level, the rightmost node.
- **Level-size snapshot** – capture `queue.size()` at each level's start, drain that many nodes, and record the last.
- **Not the right spine** – the rightmost node per level may come from the left subtree if the right subtree is shorter.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time, O(w) space for BFS; O(n) time, O(h) space for DFS.
- **Symmetric** – the left view captures the first node per level instead.
s1_definition.analogy: Looking at the National Bank of India approval tree from the right edge, you see only the rightmost approver on each rank, because they block the view of everyone to their left on that rank. Collecting the rightmost approver per rank top to bottom is the right view.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  BFS Right View

       CEO          Level 0: last = CEO
      /   \
    VP1   VP2       Level 1: last = VP2
   /
  DIR1              Level 2: last = DIR1

  Right view: [CEO, VP2, DIR1]
  Note: DIR1 is a left child but rightmost at level 2
```

```text
  DFS Right-First Visit Order

  Visit: CEO(0) → VP2(1) → VP1(1,skip) → DIR1(2)
  Result builds: [CEO] → [CEO,VP2] → [CEO,VP2,DIR1]
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The right view of a binary tree is the last node of each level, which is what you see standing on the right side. You compute it with BFS and the level-size snapshot: enqueue the root, snapshot the queue size at each iteration, drain that many nodes, and capture the one at index `levelSize - 1`.

The crucial insight is that the right view is not the right spine. If the left subtree runs deeper than the right, the last node on a deeper level comes from the left side. The level-based last-node rule handles this automatically.

The DFS alternative visits the right child first and records the first node seen at each new depth, using O(h) space instead of O(w). The symmetric left view captures the first node per level instead of the last.

In our banking system at National Bank of India, the right view produces a summary of the most senior fallback approver at each escalation rank. Some ranks have no right-side branch, so the visible approver is a left-side node, and the level-based rule correctly includes those fallbacks.

Remember one sentence: BFS level-size snapshot, capture the last node per level; that is the right view, not just the right spine.
